claims.text: The starting material is additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 with a predominantly fcc matrix.
The starting alloy exhibits high strength and fatigue performance.
Elevated-temperature degradation of this alloy is primarily controlled by selective oxidation of Al and Ti.
Al and Ti are the reactive elements principally responsible for oxide formation in this alloy.
An oxidizing atmosphere causes Al and Ti to form a continuous, adherent, protective scale containing Al2O3 and/or TiO2.
The continuous oxide scale acts as a barrier to further degradation.
The protective scale preserves the underlying fcc microstructure and mechanical integrity.
A reducing or hydrogen-enriched atmosphere produces a thinner or discontinuous oxide scale because insufficient oxygen is available.
A deficient scale under reducing conditions permits enhanced internal oxidation.
Internal oxidation under reducing conditions causes microstructural destabilization and eventually compromises alloy integrity.
Exposure at 900–1000 °C for several hours can develop an oxide scale while remaining below the threshold for extensive bulk phase transformation.
Samples exposed to an oxidizing atmosphere will have lower overall mass gain than samples exposed to a reducing atmosphere.
Oxidizing exposure will cause minimal changes in mechanical properties relative to the starting-state baseline.
Reducing exposure will produce incomplete or less-protective scales, greater internal oxidation, and higher or more irregular mass changes.
Reducing exposure will cause measurable losses in mechanical performance relative to the unexposed baseline.
Interactions among alloying elements can affect oxidation resistance and oxidation kinetics in compositionally complex alloys.
Identically processed specimens exposed at the same temperature and duration under oxidizing and reducing atmospheres provide a controlled comparison of redox effects.
Mass change, scale composition and continuity, internal-oxidation depth, and mechanical properties are measurable discriminating variables.

Statistically indistinguishable scale characteristics and mechanical degradation between the two atmospheres, or a similarly protective scale in the reducing atmosphere, would falsify the proposed control mechanism.

contradictions.description: The conditions and boundary state that exposure will preserve the fcc microstructure and remain below phase-transformation thresholds, while the mediator explicitly includes phase alterations and the mechanism predicts microstructural destabilization under reducing exposure. The hypothesis does not distinguish permissible near-surface changes from excluded bulk transformations.
